Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
A specific texture associated with the event

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette: Elena, a fifty-five-year-old divorced Latin American woman, spent her early thirties in a combat zone where a sudden explosion tore through her forward operating base. She remembers the specific grit of ash and shredded canvas under her boots, the concussive bang that left her ears ringing, and the sight of close comrades lost to the shrapnel. The memory of that afternoon never settled into a coherent timeline. When she tried to explain what happened to coworkers over the years, she would lose the thread entirely, her words tangling over an event she could not put in the right order. The account grew so extreme and disjointed that she found it increasingly difficult to believe it had actually happened to her. Now, Elena works as a bank teller behind a reinforced glass window. The moment a customer begins recounting how they lost a loved one to a sudden illness, the conversation acts as a direct fuse. The trigger immediately floods her with physical reactivity; her chest tightens, her breathing becomes shallow, and her palms sweat against the counter. That same trigger pulls the fractured combat memories forward, pulling the past into the present and distorting her perception of the room. As the past bleeds through, Elena's negative appraisals take root: she starts to believe the world is a dangerous place and convinces herself that she has to be on guard at all times. The constant threat monitoring quickly becomes the engine of her decline. Because she studies every face in the waiting line and constantly scans for danger, her nervous system stays locked in a state of high alert. This sustained physical and cognitive reactivity reinforces her negative appraisals, convincing her that nothing in her life feels meaningful anymore and that survival is the only worthwhile pursuit. The threat state, in turn, becomes hypersensitive, causing ordinary bank sounds to register as imminent warnings. A heavy vault door slamming shut or a delivery truck backing up on the street instantly reactivates the trigger, sending her into a fresh spiral. When the combat memories resurface, they amplify the threat response, making her flinch at the hiss of the coffee machine or the texture of a deposit slip's rough paper, which then pulls the trigger response back to the surface. The cycle tightened over months. She began avoiding the main lobby, requested a transfer to the basement archives, and stopped returning calls from an ex-husband who tried to visit, fearing that one moment of lowered vigilance would cost her everything. She had come to believe that her daily life held no purpose beyond maintaining a state of constant readiness. The exhaustion of perpetual surveillance finally outpaced her fear. Last month, Elena walked into a community mental health clinic, holding a manila folder of deployment records she still could not fully articulate. She hopes the therapist might help her piece together the sequence of her memories without feeling as though she is reliving the blast, and she is most afraid that if she ever stops scanning for danger, she will be caught completely unprepared.
